pages.text: At the market, Rahmatu helped her Auntie Husseina sell fish. “If we do not sell the fresh fish today,” said Auntie, “it will spoil. In warm weather, fresh fish can go bad within a day.” Rahmatu asked, “Why does food go bad?”
sentences: At the market, Rahmatu helped her Auntie Husseina sell fish.
“If we do not sell the fresh fish today,” said Auntie, “it will spoil.
In warm weather, fresh fish can go bad within a day.” Rahmatu asked, “Why does food go bad?”
pages.alt: At a tidy Ghanaian market stall, Rahmatu stands beside Auntie Husseina, who arranges shiny fresh silver fish on crushed ice alongside baskets of golden smoked fish.

pages.text: “Tiny living things called germs grow on food, especially when it is warm and wet,” said Auntie. “They make the food smell bad, feel slimy or grow mould. Food that has spoiled can make you ill.”
sentences: “Tiny living things called germs grow on food, especially when it is warm and wet,” said Auntie.
“They make the food smell bad, feel slimy or grow mould.
Food that has spoiled can make you ill.”
pages.alt: Auntie Husseina explaining carefully to Rahmatu, comparing fresh bright fish kept cool in a bowl of ice with a separate old piece set aside for disposal.

pages.text: “Dry food keeps longer because germs need water to grow,” said Auntie. She laid clean fish out on raised racks in the bright sun to dry. “Drying takes the water out.”
sentences: “Dry food keeps longer because germs need water to grow,” said Auntie.
She laid clean fish out on raised racks in the bright sun to dry.
“Drying takes the water out.”
pages.alt: In a clean sunlit courtyard, Auntie Husseina lays neat rows of small silver fish on a raised mesh drying table under the warm sun while Rahmatu watches.

pages.text: Auntie also smoked fish on a wire rack over a clay smoking oven, watching the heat carefully herself. “Smoking dries the fish and helps keep it,” she said. “Salting works the same way. And cold keeps germs from growing quickly, which is why we keep fresh fish on ice or in a refrigerator.”
sentences: Auntie also smoked fish on a wire rack over a clay smoking oven, watching the heat carefully herself.
“Smoking dries the fish and helps keep it,” she said.
“Salting works the same way.
And cold keeps germs from growing quickly, which is why we keep fresh fish on ice or in a refrigerator.”
pages.alt: Auntie Husseina tending golden-brown fish on a raised wire tray atop a traditional Ghanaian clay Chorkor smoking oven with gentle smoke rising while Rahmatu stands safely back.

pages.text: “Even so, we must always check our food,” said Auntie. “If food smells bad, feels slimy or has mould, do not eat it. Tell a grown-up and throw it away. Keep dried and smoked fish in a dry, clean, covered basket, wash your hands before and after touching fish, and cook fish well before eating it.”

pages.alt: Rahmatu washing her hands with soap at a basin beside neatly covered woven baskets of golden smoked fish on a clean counter while Auntie Husseina nods.

pages.text: Rahmatu wrote a summary for her class: “Food goes bad because germs grow on it. We can dry, smoke, salt or cool food to keep it longer. Always check food before eating it, and keep it clean and covered.” Auntie Husseina smiled. “You will be a wonderful teacher.”

activities.question: What should you do with food that smells bad or has mould?
options: Not eat it and tell a grown-up

activities.prompt: Put the fish in order, from the market stall to the cooking pot.
items: Keep the fresh fish cool, on ice, at the stall.
Smoke or dry the fish while an adult watches the fire.
Store the dried fish in a dry, clean, covered place.
Wash your hands, check the smell, and cook the fish well.

activities.definition: To go bad so that you cannot eat it safely.
